issues.subcategory: sample contradiction (student vs. national probability sample)
issues.description: The abstract, introduction, and discussion repeatedly describe the data as coming from a 'national probability sample' that is 'nationally representative.' However, the Methods section states participants were recruited from an introductory psychology participant pool, with a mean age of 19 and 68% female. This is a convenience student sample, not a national probability sample. This contradiction is fatal to the paper's central argument, because the entire interpretation hinges on contrasting their 'general population' findings (SDO stronger) with a prior student-sample study (RWA stronger). If the sample is actually a student pool, the key explanatory framework collapses.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington. This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013). Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1

issues.description: The claim of high generalizability rests on the sample being nationally representative, which directly conflicts with the Methods description of an undergraduate participant pool. A 19-year-old, 86% Pākehā, university student sample cannot support claims of representativeness of the New Zealand population.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The title, abstract, and discussion frame the outcome as 'willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment' or 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment' (WILL). However, the actual measure is described as environmental concern, with two items asking how concerned participants are and whether problems are exaggerated. Concern is not the same construct as behavioral willingness/sacrifice, so the central dependent variable is mislabeled throughout, undermining the interpretation of all findings.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, “How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?” and “To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?”.

issues.description: The authors' own model-comparison test (their substitute for the Wald test) showed no significant difference between the SDO→environmentalism and RWA→environmentalism paths (Δχ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126). Despite failing to reject the null of equal predictive strength, they conclude SDO is the stronger predictor based merely on the 'pattern of unstandardized coefficients.' This is a direct contradiction of their own hypothesis test and constitutes the main (unsupported) conclusion of the paper.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.subcategory: unjustified causal inference from cross-lagged data
issues.description: Cross-lagged panel models cannot establish causation, and the traditional CLPM does not separate between-person and within-person variance (a known limitation addressed by random-intercept models). Yet the authors make repeated strong causal claims. This overinterpretation is inconsistent with the correlational, observational design, especially given they themselves note a possible third-variable explanation.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.

issues.description: Listwise deletion was used across five waves. With longitudinal panel data this discards all participants with any missing wave, reduces statistical power, and can bias estimates if attrition is non-random (very likely over five years). Modern approaches (FIML/multiple imputation) are standard for such data and would be expected here. No analysis of attrition or comparison of completers vs. dropouts is reported.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.subcategory: inconsistency between reported N and confidence intervals
issues.description: The reported N is 374, yet the confidence intervals for means are implausibly narrow (e.g., 2.60 [2.58, 2.63]). With N=374 and SD≈0.96, the 95% CI half-width should be roughly ±0.10, not ±0.025. The reported intervals imply an effective N in the thousands, suggesting the actual analytic sample differs from the stated 374 (possibly the full NZAVS database). This inconsistency casts doubt on the reported sample and the precision of all estimates.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1

issues.description: The Data Analysis section states a significance threshold of p < .05, but the Figure 1 caption states the threshold is p < .01. These contradictory thresholds make it unclear how 'significance' was determined for the reported paths and reduces transparency.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.description: CFI = .86 is below conventional acceptable thresholds (.90/.95) and indicates poor fit. The authors dismiss this as an artifact of 'model complexity' and accept the model based only on RMSEA and SRMR. The χ²/df ratio is large. The justification for accepting a poorly fitting model is weak and should be explicitly tested rather than asserted.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: Reliabilities are marginal (SDO = .69, RWA = .70, WILL = .76 with only two items), acknowledged by the authors as poorer than usual. Low reliability attenuates observed associations and can distort relative comparisons between SDO and RWA—precisely the comparison the paper rests on. The two-item environmental measure is especially weak.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.subcategory: measurement invariance / changing items across waves
issues.description: One RWA item was not assessed at Time 2 but was included at all other waves. Combined with constraining residual variances to equality across time, this raises a measurement invariance problem: the RWA construct is operationalized with different items across waves, which can bias autoregressive and cross-lagged estimates. No formal test of longitudinal measurement invariance (loadings/intercepts) is reported.
issues.quote: The item “Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done”, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The Data Analysis section states standardized parameters are presented, while the Figure 1 caption and the Results report unstandardized B coefficients. This internal contradiction makes it unclear which metric underlies the comparisons between SDO and RWA effects, which is central to the conclusions.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances.

issues.description: Path estimates are reported with 'SD' (e.g., B = -.11, SD = .01). For regression/path coefficients this should be the standard error (SE), not a standard deviation. Mislabeling makes the precision of estimates ambiguous.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: The description of model constraints repeats the same sentence about constraining cross-lagged associations to equality at both the start and end of the paragraph, creating confusion about which constraints were actually imposed and in what order. This undermines replicability of the analytic model.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points. Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.subcategory: stationarity assumption and unequal time intervals
issues.description: The model imposes time-invariant (stationary) cross-lagged effects, assuming the strength of effects is constant across the entire interval, but this assumption is not tested or justified empirically. Additionally, the title claims 'five-year' while the Methods describe 'five semesters (2009 to 2013),' leaving the actual measurement intervals unclear. Cross-lagged estimates are sensitive to lag length, so unequal/ambiguous intervals threaten interpretation.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.description: Several 'significant' effects are extremely small (e.g., RWA→environmentalism B = -.02; willingness→RWA B = -.01; SDO→RWA B ≈ -.001). With a possibly very large effective N, statistical significance does not imply meaningful effects. The paper interprets these tiny coefficients substantively (e.g., bidirectionality, socialization into authoritarianism) without addressing practical significance.
issues.quote: The lagged effect of willingness to sacrifice on both SDO and RWA were statistically significant and negative (B = -.04, SD = .002, p < .001, 95% CI [-.04, -.03] and B = -.01, SD = .002, p = .002, 95% CI [-.01, -.003], respectively).

issues.description: Numerous chi-square difference tests and path significance tests are conducted (path equality, directionality, SDO-RWA reciprocity) without any adjustment for multiple comparisons, increasing the risk of false positives among the many reported tests.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001), a finding we explore more fully in the Discussion.

issues.subcategory: post hoc reinterpretation of disconfirmed hypothesis
issues.description: The authors predicted reciprocal bidirectional SDO–RWA effects, but found RWA predicted SDO while SDO did not predict RWA. Rather than treating this as a disconfirmation, they reinterpret it post hoc (New Zealanders being 'socialized into authoritarianism') in a way not anticipated and not directly testable with these data. This risks HARKing/over-interpretation of an unexpected null path.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.description: The method is described as 'path analysis' (implying observed composites), yet the constraints discuss item-level residual variances across time, implying a latent variable/CFA structure with multiple indicators. It is unclear whether SDO, RWA, and environmentalism were modeled as latent factors or observed scores, which materially affects how estimates, fit indices, and reliabilities should be interpreted and reproduced.
issues.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment. The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus

issues.description: Key details (retention/attrition across waves, exact timing of waves, how the 374 were selected, response/retention rates) are deferred entirely to an external website rather than reported, limiting transparency and replicability—particularly important given the attrition concerns with listwise deletion over five years.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.
